name: Display refresh rate (measured)
plain: Estimated by timing animation frames; 60, 90, 120 or 144 Hz.
meaning: No API reports refresh rate; scripts measure the gap between requestAnimationFrame callbacks. Distinguishes high-refresh phones and gaming monitors, but is noisy under load.

web.api: requestAnimationFrame timestamp deltas over about 1 second

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can estimate your screen's refresh rate by timing about one second of animation
limits.user_action: Nothing. It runs for about a second when the page loads or an animation starts.
can: Count animation frames to guess 60, 90, 120 or 144 Hz
Tune animations and games to match
Add the result to a browser fingerprint
cannot: Get an exact value, since busy or power saving devices give slightly wrong numbers
Measure while the tab is hidden

story.what_it_is: A page estimates how fast your screen redraws, such as 60, 120 or 144 times a second.
story.for_you: You never see the test. The page counts how quickly the screen redraws. It is why a game can feel smoother on a fast gaming screen.
story.for_makers: Games use it to set a smooth frame rate and spare weak devices. Ad and fraud teams use it too, because real screens redraw in a steady rhythm and bots often do not.

use_cases.example: A browser game matches its frame rate to a 120 Hz display so motion looks silky.
A cloud gaming site asks the server for a stream at 60 or 120 frames to match your screen.
A video player picks smoother playback modes on high refresh screens.
A drawing app updates ink as fast as the screen allows, so pen strokes feel instant.
A bot check sees a browser with odd frame timing, such as a virtual machine or a headless browser.
A measurement script uses the display speed as one more clue in a device ID.
A team measures page smoothness on real devices to find slow spots.

technical_bounds: Safari low power mode caps at 30 or 60
